content: Laxatives, also known as purgatives, are substances such as foods, compounds, or medications that are used to stimulate bowel movements or soften stool. They are most commonly employed to treat constipation. Certain types of laxatives, including stimulant, lubricant, and saline laxatives, are also utilized to clear the colon in preparation for rectal and bowel examinations. In such cases, their use may be supplemented with enemas. When taken in sufficiently high doses, laxatives can induce diarrhea. However, it is important to note that laxatives primarily act on the large intestine and colon to expedite the elimination of undigested food residues. Laxatives are available in various forms, including oral preparations and suppositories. Some laxatives combine multiple active ingredients to achieve a combination of effects. While the prevalence of laxative use shows gender differences, with females being more commonly affected than males, the physiological mechanisms by which laxatives function do not differ significantly between genders. Marketing strategies for laxatives often target these gender differences, with some brands promoting their products as more feminine. Certain foods and vegetables are known to have natural laxative properties and can be consumed to alleviate constipation. These include almonds, aloe vera, apple juice, beets, chicken broth, chicory, chocolate, coconut, coffee, dandelion, dates, dried apricots, endive, figs, flaxseed, grapes, hot tea with lemon, licorice, mangos, molasses, olives, papayas, parsley, peaches, pears, persimmons, pineapples, plums, prunes, rhubarb, soybeans, spicy foods, turnips, walnuts, and watercress. The effectiveness of these natural remedies may vary among individuals. Bulk-producing agents, also referred to as bulking agents or roughage, act on both the small and large intestines. They typically take 12 to 72 hours to produce an effect. Examples include psyllium husk (Metamucil), methylcellulose (Citrucel), polycarbophil, dietary fiber, and apples. These agents increase stool bulk and water retention, forming an emollient gel that facilitates easier movement of stool through the intestines via peristalsis. They are considered the gentlest type of laxatives and are often used to maintain regular bowel movements. Adequate water intake is essential when using bulk-producing agents. Stool softeners, also known as surfactants, act on the small and large intestines and have an onset of action of 12 to 72 hours. Examples include docusate (Colace, Diocto). These agents allow water and fats to penetrate the stool, making it easier to pass. However, prolonged use can lead to tolerance, reducing their effectiveness. Stool softeners are intermediate in strength between bulk producers and stimulant laxatives. They are particularly useful for patients with occasional constipation or those with anorectal conditions where passing firm stool is painful. Lubricants, such as mineral oil, act primarily on the colon and have an onset of action of 6 to 8 hours. These agents make the stool slippery, facilitating its passage through the intestines. Mineral oil also reduces colonic water absorption, further softening the stool. However, it may interfere with the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K). Hydrating agents, also known as osmotic laxatives, work by increasing water retention in the intestines, thereby softening the stool. These agents are divided into saline and hyperosmotic types. Saline laxatives, such as magnesium citrate, magnesium hydroxide (Milk of Magnesia), and Epsom salt (magnesium sulfate), attract and retain water in the intestinal lumen, increasing intraluminal pressure and softening stool. They also stimulate the release of cholecystokinin, which aids in the digestion of fats and proteins. However, saline laxatives can disrupt fluid and electrolyte balance. Hyperosmotic agents, such as lactulose, sorbitol, glycerin suppositories, and polyethylene glycol (PEG), act by retaining water in the colon and stimulating colonic peristalsis. Lactulose is also used to treat portal-systemic encephalopathy. PEG solutions, often combined with electrolytes, are used for whole bowel irrigation in preparation for surgery or colonoscopy and for treating certain types of poisoning. Brand names include GoLYTELY, GlycoLax, CoLyte, and NuLYTELY. Stimulant laxatives act on the colon by stimulating peristaltic action. They are the most potent type of laxatives and should only be used in extreme cases. Long-term use can lead to cathartic colon, a condition characterized by reduced colonic function due to overstimulation. These laxatives act on the intestinal mucosa or nerve plexus and alter water and electrolyte secretion. Castor oil, which acts on the small intestine, is sometimes preferred for more complete evacuation. It is converted into ricinoleic acid, the active component, in the gut. Serotonin agonists, such as tegaserod, stimulate gastrointestinal motility by activating 5-HT4 receptors in the enteric nervous system. However, their use requires caution due to potential cardiovascular side effects. Laxatives are used for various purposes, including bowel preparation for medical procedures, managing chronic constipation, and addressing issues related to chronic immobility. However, laxative abuse can lead to serious complications, such as intestinal paralysis, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), pancreatitis, renal failure, and other health problems. Chronic use of stimulant laxatives is particularly concerning, as it may cause colonic tissues to become less responsive over time, potentially leading to dependency. A common finding in patients with chronic stimulant laxative use is melanosis coli, a condition characterized by brown pigmentation of the intestinal tissue. Laxatives are also frequently misused by individuals with eating disorders, such as bulimia nervosa, as a means of purging food before it is digested. Many of these individuals have a history of chronic digestive problems and may have initially used laxatives as an effective treatment. Over time, laxative use may replace more appropriate treatments, such as dietary modifications. Treating patients with eating disorders and associated gastrointestinal issues can be particularly challenging.
